vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus sits with his hands folded in his lap, shoulders tensed despite the warmth of the office. At thirty-two, he has the weathered appearance of someone who spends most days outdoors, though lately those days have become fewer. He works as a park ranger in a national forest, a job he loved for nearly a decade before everything changed.

Three years ago, Marcus was on a solo backcountry patrol when he encountered a group of men illegally mining in a remote canyon. What started as a routine confrontation escalated. They overpowered him, took him to an abandoned structure, and held him for four days. During that time, they beat him repeatedly, withheld water, and threatened him with tools. They wanted information about ranger patrol patterns. Marcus gave them nothing, but the cost was measured in ways that still haven't fully healed.

He was found by a search party after missing his check-in. The physical injuries resolved within months—broken ribs, lacerations, a dislocated shoulder. The other injuries proved more persistent.

Marcus describes his current life in measured tones, as though narrating someone else's experience. He still works as a ranger, though his supervisor has noticed changes. He takes only day shifts now, refusing any overnight assignments. The thought of being alone in the backcountry—the very landscape he once found peaceful—now triggers a cascade of physical sensations: his chest tightens, his vision narrows, and an urgent need to escape overwhelms him. He's had to turn down promotions that would require remote fieldwork.

At night, Marcus rarely sleeps more than a few hours. When he does sleep, he dreams of that canyon—sometimes exactly as it was, sometimes distorted into something more sinister. He wakes gasping, his sheets soaked with sweat, his body convinced he's still trapped. On bad nights, he doesn't try to sleep at all. Instead, he sits in his apartment with lights on, scrolling through his phone or watching television, anything to keep his mind occupied.

His apartment has become smaller in some ways. He's hypervigilant to sounds—a car backfiring on the street outside sends his heart racing. He locks his doors multiple times before bed, checking them again at midnight, 3 a.m., and 5 a.m. When colleagues approach him unexpectedly at work, he startles violently. One coworker joked about it once; Marcus hasn't made eye contact with that person since.

He's isolated himself gradually, almost without noticing. Friends stopped inviting him out after he cancelled plans repeatedly. Dating feels impossible—he can't imagine being vulnerable with another person, can't imagine explaining why he sometimes freezes when touched. His family calls regularly, but he keeps conversations brief and superficial. They don't understand, and he doesn't have the energy to help them understand.

Marcus knows intellectually that he survived, that he's safe now. But his body hasn't received that message. He remains hyperaware of exits in every room, of people's hands, of situations where he might be trapped. The confidence he once had in his own competence has fractured. He questions his judgment constantly, replays decisions from that day obsessively, wondering what he could have done differently.

What troubles him most is the loss of who he was. He's still breathing, still functioning, still showing up to work. But the man who loved solitude in wild places, who felt alive in remote forests, feels like a stranger to him now. That version of Marcus seems impossibly distant.
